en: Netti: The Section on Detailed Exposition (Paṭiniddesavāra) – Part One I. The Section on the Four Truths (Cattārisaccavibhaṅga) 1. The Truth of Suffering (Dukkhasacca) What is the Truth of Suffering? It is the five aggregates subject to clinging. What five? They are: the aggregate of material form subject to clinging, the aggregate of feeling subject to clinging, the aggregate of perception subject to clinging, the aggregate of mental formations subject to clinging, and the aggregate of consciousness subject to clinging. 2. The Truth of the Origin of Suffering (Dukkhasamudayasacca) What is the Truth of the Origin of Suffering? It is craving, which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there; that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. 3. The Truth of the Cessation of Suffering (Dukkhanirodhasacca) What is the Truth of the Cessation of Suffering? It is the remainderless fading away and cessation of that same craving, giving it up, relinquishing it, letting it go, and not relying on it. 4. The Truth of the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering (Dukkhanirodhagāminīpaṭipadāsacca) What is the Truth of the Way Leading to the Cessation of Suffering?

It is this Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. II. The Section on the Four Nutriments (Cattāro āhārā vibhaṅga) 1. Physical Nutriment (Kabaḷīkāra-āhāra) What is physical nutriment? It is the substance that is edible, chewable, drinkable, and tastable, which enters the stomach and provides nourishment. 2. Contact as Nutriment (Phassa-āhāra) What is contact as nutriment? It is the six classes of contact: contact with the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. 3. Mental Volition as Nutriment (Manosañcetanā-āhāra) What is mental volition as nutriment? It is the six classes of volitional formations: volition regarding forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena. 4. Consciousness as Nutriment (Viññāṇa-āhāra) What is consciousness as nutriment? It is the six classes of consciousness: eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness. III. The Section on the Four Bases of Accomplishment (Cattāro iddhipādā vibhaṅga) 1. The Base of Accomplishment Constituted by Concentration of Desire (Chandiddhipāda) What is the base of accomplishment constituted by concentration of desire? Herein, a bhikkhu develops the basis for spiritual power that possesses concentration due to desire and is accompanied by volitional formations, thinking: "May my body be thus, may my body be not thus. This is called the base of accomplishment constituted by concentration of desire. 2. The Base of Accomplishment Constituted by Concentration of Energy (Vīriyiddhipāda) What is the base of accomplishment constituted by concentration of energy? Herein, a bhikkhu develops the basis for spiritual power that possesses concentration due to energy and is accompanied by volitional formations, thinking: "May my body be thus, may my body be not thus. This is called the base of accomplishment constituted by concentration of energy. 3. The Base of Accomplishment Constituted by Concentration of Mind (Citiddhipāda) What is the base of accomplishment constituted by concentration of mind? Herein, a bhikkhu develops the basis for spiritual power that possesses concentration due to mind and is accompanied by volitional formations, thinking: "May my body be thus, may my body be not thus. This is called the base of accomplishment constituted by concentration of mind. 4. The Base of Accomplishment Constituted by Concentration of Investigation (Vīmaṃsiddhipāda) What is the base of accomplishment constituted by concentration of investigation? Herein, a bhikkhu develops the basis for spiritual power that possesses concentration due to investigation and is accompanied by volitional formations, thinking: "May my body be thus, may my body be not thus. This is called the base of accomplishment constituted by concentration of investigation. IV. The Section on the Four Foundations of Mindfulness (Cattāro satipaṭṭhānā vibhaṅga) 1. Contemplation of the Body (Kāyānupassanā) What is contemplation of the body? Herein, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body internally, externally, or both internally and externally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. This is called contemplation of the body. 2. Contemplation of Feelings (Vedanānupassanā) What is contemplation of feelings? Herein, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating feelings in feelings internally, externally, or both internally and externally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. This is called contemplation of feelings. 3. Contemplation of the Mind (Cittānupassanā) What is contemplation of the mind? Herein, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the mind in the mind internally, externally, or both internally and externally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. This is called contemplation of the mind. 4. Contemplation of Phenomena (Dhammānupassanā) What is contemplation of phenomena? Herein, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena internally, externally, or both internally and externally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. This is called contemplation of phenomena. V. The Section on the Four Right Strivings (Cattāro sammappadhānā vibhaṅga) 1. The Right Striving for the Non-Arising of Unarisen Evil Unwholesome States What is the right striving for the non-arising of unarisen evil unwholesome states? Herein, a bhikkhu generates will, makes an effort, stirs up energy, exerts his mind, and strives so that unarisen evil unwholesome states do not arise. This is called the right striving for the non-arising of unarisen evil unwholesome states. 2. The Right Striving for the Abandoning of Arisen Evil Unwholesome States What is the right striving for the abandoning of arisen evil unwholesome states? Herein, a bhikkhu generates will, makes an effort, stirs up energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the abandoning of arisen evil unwholesome states. This is called the right striving for the abandoning of arisen evil unwholesome states. 3. The Right Striving for the Arising of Unarisen Wholesome States What is the right striving for the arising of unarisen wholesome states? Herein, a bhikkhu generates will, makes an effort, stirs up energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the arising of unarisen wholesome states. This is called the right striving for the arising of unarisen wholesome states. 4. The Right Striving for the Maintenance of Arisen Wholesome States What is the right striving for the maintenance of arisen wholesome states?

Herein, a bhikkhu generates will, makes an effort, stirs up energy, exerts his mind, and strives for the maintenance, non-confusion, increase, expansion, and fulfillment by development of arisen wholesome states. This is called the right striving for the maintenance of arisen wholesome states. VI. The Section on the Four Bases of Psychic Power (Cattāro iddhipādā vibhaṅga) [This section is identical to the previous Section III. VII. The Section on the Four Jhānas (Cattāri jhānāni vibhaṅga) 1. The First Jhāna What is the first jhāna? Herein, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, a bhikkhu enters upon and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. This is called the first jhāna. 2. The Second Jhāna What is the second jhāna? With the stilling of applied and sustained thought, a bhikkhu enters upon and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, is without applied and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of concentration. The Analysis of the Mode of Conveying Teaching (Desanāhāravibhaṅga). Therein, what is the mode of conveying teaching?
The verse beginning with “Through gratification and danger” is this mode of conveying teaching.
What does he teach?
He teaches the gratification, the danger, the escape, the fruit, the means, and the instruction.

“Monks, I shall teach you the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with its meaning and its phrasing; I shall reveal the holy life, entirely complete and pure.”
In this regard, what is the gratification?
“When one who desires sensual pleasures succeeds in obtaining them...”
“Truly, a mortal becomes joyful in mind when he obtains what he desires.
This is the gratification.
In this regard, what is the danger?
"If for that person who desires sensual pleasures,
who has conceived a longing for them..."
“Those sensual pleasures fade away,
and one is tormented as if pierced by an arrow.
This is the disadvantage.
In this regard, what is the escape?
"He who avoids sensual pleasures as one would the head of a snake with his foot— "
“Mindful, one overcomes the attachment to existence in the world.
This is the escape.
In this regard, what is the gratification?
"Fields, lands, or gold;
cattle, horses, slaves, and servants;"
“The woman’s kinsmen are manifold desires;
the man who greedily clings to them”—
this is the gratification.
In that regard, what is the danger?
"The weak overpower him,
and perils crush him."
Then suffering follows him,
like water entering a broken boat.
This is the disadvantage.
In this regard, what is the escape?
"Therefore, a person who is always mindful should avoid sensual pleasures."
"Having abandoned these, cross the flood,
like one who has boarded a boat and reached the further shore.
This is the escape.
In this regard, what is the fruit?
“The Dhamma indeed protects the one who lives by the Dhamma,
like a great umbrella in the time of rain.”
“This is the benefit when the Dhamma is well-practiced:
one who lives according to the Dhamma does not go to a state of misery.
This is the fruit.
In this regard, what is the means?
“All conditioned phenomena are impermanent,” … [and so on] …
“All conditioned phenomena are suffering,” …pe… “All phenomena are non-self.”
When one sees with wisdom,
then one becomes disenchanted with suffering;
this is the path to purification.
This is the means.
In this regard, what is the instruction?
"Just as one with eyes [avoids] uneven ground..."
While there is still effort to be made,
let the wise person in this world of living beings avoid all evils.”
This is the instruction.
In this regard, what is the fruit?
"Behold the world as empty;... [and so forth]."
“Mogharāja” is the command;
“Always mindful” is the means;
“Having uprooted the view of self.”
"In this way, one may become a crosser over death.
This is the fruit.
Therein, the Blessed One teaches the escape for the person who understands through a condensed statement, and for the person who understands through an elaborated explanation.
He teaches the danger and the escape; he teaches the gratification, the danger, and the escape for a person who is to be guided.
In this regard, there are four modes of practice and four types of persons.

One who is dominated by craving and is dull-witted is led out by means of the foundations of mindfulness as supports, through the painful mode of practice with sluggish direct knowledge, by means of the faculty of mindfulness.
One of craving-temperament who is energetic is led out by means of the faculty of concentration, via a painful practice and quick direct knowledge, supported by the jhānas.
One of view-temperament who is dull is led out by means of the faculty of energy, via a pleasant practice and sluggish direct knowledge, supported by the right endeavors.
One of view-temperament who is energetic is led out by means of the faculty of wisdom, via a pleasant practice and quick direct knowledge, supported by the truths.
Both those of craving-temperament are led out by insight preceded by serenity toward the liberation of mind through the fading away of lust.
Both those of view-temperament are led out by serenity preceded by insight toward the liberation by wisdom through the fading away of ignorance.

In this regard, those who are led out by practices preceded by serenity should be applied by means of the "hook-turning" method (*nandiyāvaṭṭa-naya*); those who are led out by practices preceded by insight should be applied by means of the "lion’s play" method (*sīhavikkīḷita-naya*).
Where does this necklace originate? It originates from the Teacher teaching the Dhamma, or from a certain venerable fellow-celibate; having heard that Dhamma, one acquires faith.
In that regard, whatever investigation, exertion, weighing, and examination there is, this is wisdom consisting of what has been heard (*sutamayī paññā*).
Likewise, whatever investigation, weighing, examination, and mental scrutiny there is based on that which has been heard as a support, this is wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī paññā*).

The knowledge that arises for one associated with attention through these two types of wisdom—whether on the plane of seeing or the plane of development—is wisdom consisting in development (*bhāvanāmayī paññā*).
Wisdom consisting in what has been heard (*sutamayī paññā*) arises from the voice of another.
Wisdom consisting in reflection (*cintāmayī paññā*) arises from wise attention directed inwardly.
The knowledge that arises through the voice of another and through wise attention directed inwardly is wisdom consisting in cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī paññā*).

One who possesses these two types of wisdom—wisdom consisting in hearing (*sutamayī*) and wisdom consisting in reflection (*cintāmayī*)—is one who understands by a condensed statement (*ugghaṭitaññū*).
One who possesses wisdom consisting in hearing but lacks wisdom consisting in reflection is one who understands by detailed exposition (*vipañcitaññū*).
One who possesses neither wisdom consisting of what has been heard nor wisdom consisting of reflection is one who must be guided (neyya).
What does this teaching of the Dhamma teach?
It teaches the Four Truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
The danger is the fruit, which is suffering; the gratification is the origin; the escape is cessation; and the means as well as the instruction is the path.
These are the four truths.
This is the Wheel of Dhamma.
As the Blessed One said:
"Monks, at Bārāṇasī, in the Deer Park at Isipatana, this 'This is suffering' was turned by me as the unsurpassed Wheel of Dhamma,
which cannot be turned back by any ascetic or brahmin, or by any deva, Māra, or Brahmā."
or whatever else exists in the world—all that is the Wheel of Dhamma.
Therein, there are immeasurable phrases, immeasurable syllables, immeasurable phonemes, immeasurable modes of expression, etymological explanations, and detailed expositions.
It is the disclosure, the manifestation, the unveiling, the analysis, the clarification, and the designation of this very meaning: "This, indeed, is the noble truth of suffering."
“‘This is the origin of suffering,’ monks—this, in Bārāṇasī at the Deer Park in Isipatana, was the unsurpassed Wheel of Dhamma set in motion by me...
‘This is the cessation of suffering,’ monks...
‘This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering,’ monks—this, in Bārāṇasī at the Deer Park in Isipatana...”
The unsurpassed Wheel of Dhamma has been set in motion, which cannot be turned back by any ascetic or brahmin,
by any deva, Māra, or Brahmā, or by anyone in the world. Therein,
there are immeasurable words, immeasurable syllables, immeasurable phonemes, immeasurable grammatical forms, and immeasurable explanations and definitions.

This is the announcement, the manifestation, the exposition, the analysis, the clarification, the definition, and the designation of this very same meaning: namely, "this is the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.

Therein, the Blessed One announces it by means of syllables (*akkhara*), manifests it by means of phrases (*pada*), exposes it by means of phonemes (*byañjana*), analyzes it by means of modes (*ākāra*), clarifies it by means of etymologies (*nirutti*), and defines it by means of detailed explanations (*niddesa*).
Therein, the Blessed One causes one to grasp it through syllables and phrases, expands upon it through phonemes and modes, and elaborates upon it through etymologies and detailed explanations.
In this context, the summary is the beginning, the exposition is the middle, and the detailed expansion is the end.
This Dhamma-Vinaya, when summarized, disciplines the person who gains knowledge through a summary; therefore, it is called "good in the beginning.
When expounded, it disciplines the person who gains knowledge through exposition; therefore, it is called "good in the middle."
By expanding upon it, he guides the person who is to be led; therefore, they say of it: "It is good in the end.
In this context, there are six factors for the meaning: revealing, manifesting, disclosing, analyzing, clarifying, and defining—these six factors constitute the meaning.
There are six factors for the phrasing: syllables, words, phrases, phonemes, modes, and designations—these six factors constitute the phrasing.
Therefore the Blessed One said: “Bhikkhus, I shall teach you the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the meaning and the phrasing.
“Entirely” (kevalaṃ) means supramundane, not mixed with mundane states.
“Perfect” (paripuṇṇaṃ) means complete, neither deficient nor redundant.
"Pure" means stainless, free from all defilements, radiant, and established as the foremost of all distinctions;
this is called the footprint of the Tathāgata, the domain frequented by the Tathāgata, and the ground colored by the Tathāgata;
it is because of this that this holy life is known.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "I shall proclaim the holy life (brahmacariya) that is entirely complete and utterly pure.
For whom is this teaching of the Dhamma? For yogis.
Therefore the Venerable Mahākaccāyana said:
“The gratification, the danger, and the escape; the fruit and the means;
and the command of the Blessed One.”
“The nutriment of teaching for yogis.
The nutriment of teaching is concluded.
